case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.limits: A narrower CFAA leaves breach of contract as the live claim. Terms of service still bind, they simply are not criminal.
case.holding: Exceeding authorised access under the CFAA means obtaining information from areas of a computer that are off limits, not using information you were entitled to obtain for a purpose the owner would dislike.

live_cases.name: Amazon.com Services, LLC v. Perplexity AI, Inc.
Amazon.com Services LLC v. Perplexity AI, Inc.

case.why_ai_cites_it: It closes the theory that violating a terms-of-service clause is a federal crime, and it is the Supreme Court backing behind the scraping practices that produced most large training corpora.

reading.body:
Van Buren established that violating terms of service is not a federal crime, and that the CFAA's "exceeds authorized access" clause requires crossing into off-limits computer areas, not misusing information you were entitled to obtain.

This distinction matters because most internet-scale training data came from scraping public pages in violation of terms of service. Before Van Buren, a company could have argued that automated data collection without permission crossed the line from breach of contract into federal crime. The ruling moved such disputes into civil contract law instead, where damages are financial and remedies narrower. This removed the criminal bar to the scraping practices that produced the training corpora underlying current large language models.

The holding does not permit scraping itself. It leaves terms of service intact as binding contracts. It only removes the criminal law theory that could have criminalized the conduct. Companies sued for scraping, as in the live Amazon v. Perplexity cases, still face breach of contract claims. Van Buren simply means they face civil liability rather than criminal prosecution. The case narrows the CFAA but does not legalize unauthorized access to information systems. What changed is the severity of the legal risk, not its existence.
